fixtures.basis: Arizona has no statewide code, so Tucson's adopted code sets the counts. Tucson adopts the 2024 International Plumbing Code and its amendment document (6 pages, read in full) changes nothing in Section 403, Table 403.1, Section 403.1.1, 403.1.2, 403.2 or 424.2. The only Chapter 4 amendments are 405.3.2 (shared lavatories for a bank of single-user rooms), 410.4 (drinking fountain substitute), new 412.13 (automatic faucets) and 423.3 (footbaths). The Tucson amendments to the 2024 International Building Code (10 pages, read in full) contain nothing on Chapter 29. So the unamended 2024 model text applies, and the Arizona state pack's model worked examples and table rows stand unchanged for Tucson. The model text was read on UpCodes' copy of the 2024 IPC as adopted by New Hampshire (secondary; UpCodes has no Tucson copy and ICC's site blocks automated access).

restrooms_city.rule: No separate city ordinance on restroom signs was found. Tucson's adopted plumbing code (2024 IPC, these sections not amended) sets both rules: single-user and family toilet rooms must be identified as available to all persons regardless of sex, and a shared room for all persons is allowed in place of separate rooms where each toilet is in a compartment with a door and each urinal is in its own partitioned area; the count for such a room is worked on 100% of the occupants. Tucson adds one amendment of its own: where gender-neutral restrooms are a continuous bank of single-user rooms, the rooms may share lavatories placed directly outside them, provided the number of lavatories is not reduced.
restrooms_city.quote: [Tucson amendment, city PDF] Section 405.3.2 Public lavatories. REVISE Section by ADDING an exception as follows: Gender neutral restroom configurations that consist of a continuous bank of single user rooms may share lavatories provided the quantity of lavatories is not reduced and the lavatories are located directly outside the single user rooms. [...] [2024 IPC 403.1.2, UpCodes copy] Single-user toilet facilities and bathing rooms, and family or assisted-use toilet facilities and bathing rooms shall be identified as being available for use by all persons regardless of their sex. [...] [2024 IPC 403.2 exception 6, UpCodes copy] Separate toilet facilities shall not be required where rooms having both water closets and lavatory fixtures are designed for use by all persons regardless of sex and privacy is provided for water closets in accordance with Section 405.3.4 and for urinals in accordance with Section 405.3.5. [405.3.4] Each water closet utilized by the public or employees shall occupy a separate compartment with walls or partitions and a door enclosing the fixtures to ensure privacy. [405.3.5] Each urinal utilized by the public or employees shall occupy a separate area with walls or partitions to provide privacy.
restrooms_city.note: One web search found no Tucson ordinance on single-user restroom signs. The Tucson City Code on American Legal Publishing returned HTTP 403 and was not searched, so absence is not confirmed.

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Tucson job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material for the desert climate and see the rules that apply.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Tucson schools, campus buildings, clinics and resorts, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.fire_bullet: - **Fire safety:** Tucson's building rules require solid plastic (HDPE) partitions to pass a fire test. Ask for the fire-rated version.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Tucson sets the number of toilets by how many people use the building, and caps how many of the men's toilets may be urinals. The table below shows what that means.
extra_rule_bullets: - **Tucson access rules:** alongside the federal standard, Tucson has adopted a national accessibility standard for buildings, in its 2017 edition.
page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** under Tucson's plumbing rules a one-person restroom must be marked as open to everyone. A shared all-gender room may take the place of separate men's and women's rooms if every toilet sits in its own compartment with a door and every urinal has its own partitioned area. Where a row of one-person rooms serves everyone, Tucson lets the rooms share sinks placed directly outside them, as long as the number of sinks is not reduced. A measure Arizona voters approved in November 2026 says that from January 1, 2027, a school or athletic association may not authorize anyone to use a restroom, locker room or shower room that is part of its athletics facilities and is not designated for that person's sex.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Tucson requires a permit to alter a building unless the work is on its exempt list, and the city says commercial tenant improvements need one. The list covers painting, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, counter tops and similar finish work, and "nonfixed and movable fixtures, cases, racks, counters and partitions not over 5 feet 9 inches" high, but it doesn't name toilet partitions. Ask Tucson Planning and Development Services whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.stalls_intro: Arizona has no statewide building rules, so Tucson's own rules decide. Tucson counts toilets by a building's capacity: the most people it is designed to hold at one time, worked out from its floor area. It isn't the number of staff or of visitors in a day. Half are counted as men and half as women. Every toilet needs a stall. Urinals are optional: in the men's room they may take the place of up to half of the toilets, or up to two thirds in restaurants and schools, so the table shows men's toilets as stalls.
page.stalls_after: These are minimums for the whole building, and at least one stall in each room must be wheelchair accessible. An office designed for 25 people or fewer, a shop designed for 100 or fewer, and any building designed for 15 or fewer, doesn't need separate men's and women's rooms. Confirm the count with Tucson Planning and Development Services.
page.capacity: To find your building's capacity, Tucson's building rules count an office at one person per 150 square feet of floor, a restaurant dining room at one per 15 square feet and a classroom at one per 20. Your architect or Tucson Planning and Development Services sets the final number.
page.install_rule: Tucson requires a licensed contractor to perform all commercial construction work, and the permit application asks for the contractor's Arizona license number. Arizona requires a state Registrar of Contractors license for commercial installation work of $1,000 or more. Confirm what your project needs with Tucson Planning and Development Services. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: A contractor on a commercial job of $1,000 or more in Arizona needs a state Registrar of Contractors license.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** Arizona has no wage law for public jobs, and state law bars cities, counties and school districts from requiring prevailing wages in their contracts. On federally funded work the federal rate applies: $33.19 an hour plus $19.20 in benefits for a carpenter on building work in Pima County.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 8.7% in Tucson: 5.6% state, 0.5% Pima County and 2.6% city.
page.buyers_extra: - **Campus buildings, resorts and spas:** finishes that match the property in guest and public restrooms, HDPE or phenolic in pool, gym and locker room restrooms that are hosed down.

Tucson has no copy on UpCodes and ICC's site blocks automated access, so the unamended parts of Tucson's code (toilet table, urinal and separate-room rules, single-user signs, floor area per person, the HDPE fire-test section, exempt items 7 and 13) were read on UpCodes' New Hampshire copy of the 2024 editions: check once in a browser at codes.iccsafe.org.

The codes page says submittals from July 1, 2026 must follow the 2024 codes; the city's January 1, 2026 news item says applications after January 1, 2026. Both dates have passed.
Tucson's permit exempt list adds work 'owned and controlled by the United States of America or the State of Arizona'; left off the page.

Tucson's own prevailing wage ordinance (2024) was ruled unenforceable by the Arizona Court of Appeals on February 27, 2026 according to news reports; not read on an official page, so not in the page text.

Tucson has a living wage for employees of contractors providing services to the city ($17.65 or $19.40 an hour in 2026, by health cover); the city's page doesn't say whether construction is covered, so it is not on the page.

Part of Tucson is in the Rio Nuevo District (the Department of Revenue lists Tucson under county codes PMA and PAD); its file gives both the same combined state and county rate (6.1%), so 8.7% holds in both. Which addresses are in the district was not checked.

Tucson also requires automatic faucets on new or replacement lavatory faucets in commercial buildings and water-saving toilets and urinals (1.28 and 0.5 gallons a flush); not about partitions, left off the page.
What ICC A117.1-2017 changes for stalls compared with the federal standard was not read; the access bullet only says both apply.
